reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of disorders of oxidative phosphorylation caused by mutations in either mitochondrial DNA or nuclear genes affecting the respiratory chain
Should be suspected when unexplained multisystem disease affects high-energy organs such as brain, muscle, heart, eye, endocrine glands, liver and kidney in unusual combinations
Mitochondrial DNA disorders are maternally inherited and show heteroplasmy, so severity and tissue involvement vary with the proportion of mutant genomes (threshold effect)

Recognisable syndromes include MELAS (stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis), MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres), Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotising encephalopathy), Kearns-Sayre and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
Elevated lactate in blood or CSF, and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, support the diagnosis but are neither fully sensitive nor specific
Muscle biopsy may show ragged-red fibres and cytochrome-c-oxidase-deficient fibres, and definitive diagnosis increasingly relies on genetic testing of mitochondrial and nuclear genomes
There is no curative therapy; management is largely supportive with cofactor and antioxidant cocktails, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins, and treatment of organ-specific complications
Certain metabolic markers may appear on newborn screening, but most mitochondrial disorders are not reliably detected by standard screening
reference.pathophysiology: Mitochondrial diseases arise from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, the process by which the electron transport chain generates ATP. Because mitochondria contain their own DNA encoding some respiratory chain subunits, while most subunits and assembly factors are nuclear-encoded, disease can follow maternal, autosomal or X-linked inheritance. Mutations reduce ATP production and may increase reactive oxygen species and lactate. Tissues with high energy demand are preferentially affected, and in mitochondrial DNA disorders the mixture of normal and mutant genomes within cells (heteroplasmy) and a threshold of mutant load determine which tissues manifest disease and how severely, explaining the marked clinical variability.
additionalDifferentials: Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency and other primary lactic acidoses
Organic acidaemias and fatty acid oxidation defects
Inflammatory or infectious encephalopathy and stroke (for stroke-like episodes)
Acquired causes of raised lactate (hypoperfusion, sepsis)
additionalInvestigations: Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate with lactate-to-pyruvate ratio
Plasma amino acids (alanine) and urine organic acids
Neuroimaging (MRI and MR spectroscopy showing a lactate peak; symmetrical basal ganglia or brainstem lesions in Leigh syndrome)
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry (ragged-red and COX-deficient fibres) and respiratory chain enzyme assays
Molecular testing of mitochondrial DNA and nuclear gene panels
Organ-specific assessment (echocardiography, audiometry, endocrine and ophthalmological review)
redFlags: Stroke-like episodes with encephalopathy, seizures and lactic acidosis (as in MELAS)
Acute metabolic decompensation with severe lactic acidosis
Rapidly progressive encephalopathy, respiratory failure or brainstem dysfunction in Leigh syndrome
Cardiac conduction block (e.g. in Kearns-Sayre) with risk of sudden death, and status epilepticus
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable, ranging from severe fatal infantile encephalopathy to slowly progressive or relatively stable adult disease, depending on the genetic defect, mutant load and organs involved; most forms are progressive with no cure, and management aims to preserve function and prevent decompensation.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal blood lactate, which can be intermittent
Using medications toxic to mitochondria (e.g. valproate in some contexts, certain antivirals) without caution
Failing to screen for treatable organ complications such as cardiac conduction disease and endocrinopathy
Overlooking maternal inheritance and the implications of heteroplasmy for family counselling
management: No curative therapy; supportive care uses a mitochondrial cofactor regimen of coenzyme Q10, riboflavin and other antioxidants with optimisation of nutrition and energy intake
Avoid mitochondrial toxins, especially sodium valproate (particularly in POLG disease) and aminoglycosides, and avoid prolonged fasting

Treat organ-specific manifestations: anticonvulsants for seizures avoiding valproate, heart-failure and pacing therapy for cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, and hormone replacement for endocrinopathies such as diabetes
Manage MELAS stroke-like episodes including consideration of L-arginine, and treat lactic acidosis and metabolic decompensation with intravenous dextrose and fluids
Structured surveillance across affected systems with echocardiography, ECG, audiometry, ophthalmology and endocrine review
Multidisciplinary specialist care coordinated through a mitochondrial disease centre, with physiotherapy, dietetics and hearing and visual rehabilitation

Genetic counselling tailored to maternal, autosomal or X-linked inheritance, with reproductive options including preimplantation genetic testing and, for mitochondrial DNA disease, mitochondrial donation
